frontmatter.title: Mode, Median, and Mean: Three Ways to Locate the Center

children.value: Intuitively speaking, the numerical measure of center is telling us what is a “typical value” of the distribution.
The three main numerical measures for the center of a distribution are the
. Each one of these measures is based on a completely different idea of describing the center of a distribution. We will first present each one of the measures, and then compare their properties.

So far, when we looked at the shape of the distribution, we identified the mode as the value where the distribution has a “peak” and saw examples when distributions have one mode (unimodal distributions) or two modes (bimodal distributions). In other words, so far we identified the mode visually from the histogram.

Technically, the mode is the most commonly occurring value in a distribution. For simple datasets where the frequency of each value is available or easily determined, the value that occurs with the highest frequency is the mode.
We will continue with the Best Actress Oscar winners example.

, age, it is helpful to list the ages in a frequency table, which gives the following results:
The mode is 33, since it occurs the most times (5).
Often, we have large sets of data and use a frequency table to display the data more efficiently.

Data were collected from the last three World Cup soccer tournaments. A total of 192 games were played. The table below lists the number of goals scored per game (not including any goals scored in shootouts).
We can see that the most frequently occurring value is 2 goals (which occurred 51 times). Therefore, the mode for this set of data is 2.

model.question: A student recorded the number of books read last month by 8 friends: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 6. What is the mode of this dataset?

choices.feedback: 2 occurs twice, but another value occurs more often.
Correct! The value 3 occurs three times, more than any other value.
6 is the largest value, not the most frequent one.

model.hint: The mode is the value that occurs most often.

children.value: Note that the mean gives a measure of center that is higher than our approximation of the center from looking at the histogram (which was about 35). The reason for this will be clear soon.
We now continue with the data from the last three World Cup soccer tournaments, displayed in the frequency table above.

To find the mean number of goals scored per game, we would need to find the sum of all 192 numbers, then divide that sum by 192. Rather than add 192 numbers, we use the fact that the same numbers appear many times. For example, the number 0 appears 17 times, the number 1 appears 45 times, the number 2 appears 51 times, etc.
If we add up 17 zeros, we get 0. If we add up 45 ones, we get 45. If we add up 51 twos, we get 102. Repeated addition is multiplication.
This way of calculating a mean is sometimes referred to as a
, since each value is “weighted” by its frequency. Note that, in this example, the values of 1, 2, and 3 are most heavily weighted.

model.question: A student's five quiz scores are 6, 8, 7, 9, and 10. What is the mean score?

choices.feedback: 7 would be the median if you ordered the values—check your sum.
40 is the sum of the scores; don't forget to divide by 5.

model.hint: Add the scores and divide by how many there are.

model.question: In 10 games, a soccer team scored 0 goals twice, 1 goal three times, and 2 goals five times. What is the mean number of goals per game?

choices.feedback: 1 is the middle value of 0, 1, 2, not the weighted mean.
13 is the total number of goals; divide by the 10 games.

model.hint: Multiply each value by its frequency, add, then divide by the total number of games.

model.question: Find the median of the dataset: 3, 5, 8, 12, 13, 14.

choices.feedback: 8 is only the 3rd observation; with an even n you must average the two center values.
Correct! The two center observations are 8 and 12, and (8 + 12)/2 = 10.
12 is only the 4th observation; average it with the 3rd.

model.hint: n = 6 is even, so average the two center observations (the 3rd and 4th).

model.question: For the dataset 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, which of the following statements is true?

choices.text: The mode and median both equal 3, and the mean equals 4
choices.feedback: Correct! The mode is 3 (most frequent), the median is 3 (middle of five ordered values), and the mean is (2+3+3+5+7)/5 = 4.

choices.text: The mode, median, and mean all equal 3
choices.feedback: Check the mean: the sum is 20 and there are 5 observations, so the mean is 4, not 3.

choices.text: The median equals 5 and the mean equals 4
choices.feedback: Check the median: the middle (3rd) observation of the ordered list is 3, not 5.

model.hint: Find all three measures: the most frequent value, the middle value, and the average.
